name: Colossus of Rhodes
description: Gigantic 33-meter bronze titan dedicated to the sun god Helios, an Ancient World Wonder.
history: Erected to commemorate the successful defense of Rhodes against a year-long siege by Demetrius Poliorcetes in 305 BCE. Financed by selling the abandoned siege engines and weaponry left behind by the besiegers.
construction: Crafted from melted siege bronze and iron over stone-weighted interior masonry towers, standing approximately 33 meters (108 feet) high at the harbor entrance.
architecture: Portrayed the sun god Helios with a radiant crown, holding a torch or spear overlooking Mandraki harbor.
significance: The tallest and most ambitious bronze statue in antiquity, inspiring future monuments including the Statue of Liberty.
currentStatus: Destroyed by the 226 BCE Rhodes earthquake after standing for only 54 years; the fallen bronze ruins lay undisturbed for 800 years until sold for scrap in 653 CE.
wonderReplacedBy: Replaced in modern global canon by the New 7 Wonders campaign
wonderHistoricalContext: Though standing for only 54 years before the 226 BCE earthquake broke its knees, an oracle warned the Rhodians against rebuilding it. Even in ruin, Pliny the Elder wrote that 'few men can clasp its thumb, and its fingers are larger than most statues.' In 653 CE, Arab caliphate forces sold the bronze to a merchant from Edessa.
